title: Calibrate a dial stem thermometer to 32 °F in ice water
instruction: Calibrate the dial thermometer in the cup of ice water so it reads 32 °F, and leave it hanging in its clip with the stem in the ice water.
context: Cooks and food prep workers (over 3 million in the US) check probe thermometers at the ice point weekly and correct them: a wrench holds the hex nut while the head is turned until the dial reads 32 °F. Unlike well-covered hold-and-turn tasks, the turn has no stop or mark: its size and direction come from reading the needle to 2 °F, valid only after the stem settles about 30 s in the water. Takes up TK-297ARY, closed for not scoring the reading.
setup: Positions: 'in front' is ahead of the line through the two arm bases, 'left'/'right' from the midline, heights above the table. (1) A clear plastic 20 oz tumbler, 13.1 cm tall, 8.6 cm across (8.0 cm inside, 3 mm wall and floor), centred 26.0 cm in front, 8.0 cm right; with its ice and water it weighs 0.45 kg (loose). Water fills it to 10.0 cm above the table; nine 2.0 to 2.2 cm ice cubes sit in it, the six at the water line at least 12 mm from the centre. (2) A stainless pot clip hooked over the tumbler's far rim, its arm reaching to a small ring at the centre: bore 7 mm, outside 10 mm, top 6 mm above the rim (13.7 cm above the table). (3) A bimetal dial stem thermometer (33 g) hanging in the ring by its hex calibration nut: a 4 mm stainless stem reaching 12.7 cm below the nut (tip 1.0 cm above the table, 9 cm of stem under water), a brass nut 10.6 mm across the flats and 7 mm tall (flats facing left and right), 4 mm of bare stem, then a stainless dial head 4.6 cm across and 1.3 cm thick. The white face reads 0 to 220 °F clockwise over 300 degrees, with ticks every 10 °F, every 2 °F from 12 to 58 °F, and a red tick at 32 °F; a black pointer. The head turns on the stem against a friction fit (0.08 N m); the pointer stays with the stem. (4) A 10.8 mm open-end steel wrench, 15.8 cm long, 4 mm thick, with a blue dipped handle (9.5 x 1.2 x 0.8 cm), 40 g, lying flat on (5) a wooden riser block 12 x 5 x 3 cm centred 17.5 cm in front, 17.0 cm left; the wrench's jaw centre is 30.0 cm in front, 17.0 cm left, its handle pointing toward the robot. The thermometer has just been stood in the ice water: it starts at room temperature and its dial is off by a set error, so in the ice it settles to a wrong reading. Lot A: room 75 °F, the dial reads 6 °F high (38 °F in ice). Lot B: room 69 °F, 9 °F low (23 °F). Lot C: room 72 °F, 4.5 °F low (27.5 °F). Nothing else changes between lots. Trials are run on lots A, B and C and averaged; the screenshot shows lot A.
scoring: Judged at the end, after at least 1 s in which nothing touches the thermometer or the wrench (no finger or gripper within 5 mm) and the thermometer, wrench and tumbler are still. 1.0 if the dial reads 32 °F within 2 °F (30 to 34), the FDA Food Code tolerance for a thermometer scaled in Fahrenheit (4-203.11(B): accurate to ±2 °F in the intended range of use). 0.5 within 4 °F (28 to 36). 0 otherwise. Either score also needs: the thermometer hanging in its clip (nut resting on the ring, at most 2 mm above it; stem within 2.5 mm of the ring's centre; at most 8 degrees from upright); the bottom 51 mm of the stem (its sensing area) under the water line for the last 30 s without a break; and the wrench put down at least 1 cm from the thermometer. 0 if the tumbler is ever tipped more than 10 degrees during the trial (ice water spills). The reading only settles in the ice: the stem takes about 30 s to cool from room temperature, and lifting the sensing area out makes it read warmer again. Turning the head while nothing holds the nut turns the whole thermometer, which does not change the reading. Trials are run on each of lots A, B and C and averaged.
reset_notes: 1. Refill the tumbler with ice and water to 10 cm above the table and set it back at its spot, clip on the far rim. 2. Warm the thermometer to room temperature, then set its error for the lot: hold the nut and turn the head until it reads 6 °F high (lot A), 9 °F low (lot B) or 4.5 °F low (lot C) against a reference thermometer in ice water, and dry it. 3. Hang it in the clip's ring with the nut's flats facing left and right, and start the trial at once. 4. Lay the wrench on the riser with its jaw toward the cup side and the handle toward the robot. 5. Arms in their ready pose.
fidelity: True size, rigid bodies (Isaac Sim, PhysX). Water is not simulated: a fixed 32 °F zone below a stated water line; the stem's temperature follows it first order (6 s, assumed) by how much of its sensing area is under water. The coil is not simulated: the drawn pointer steps by 0.5 °F; the scorer uses the exact value. One scripted catch: a seated open-end wrench locks the nut to the wrench, so the holding hand takes the head's 0.08 N m fit torque (assumed). Ice is fixed.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (mean of lots A, B and C; the arms rose and turned but never reached the wrench or the thermometer); demo: 1.0 in each lot
